passage:
"Kashish, let me tell you why I frowned at the message you showed me," said Avni. "When I was twenty-four, a stranger in a chat offered me an easy work-from-home job: rate videos, earn a fixed amount for each one. All I had to do was pay a small deposit to activate my account. It felt harmless, and the first payout even reached my bank.

"Then I got greedy. They said bigger deposits paid more, so I put in more. The account froze, and the stranger vanished. Only afterwards did I ask the question I should have asked first: why would anyone give away money for clicking? I never checked whether the company was registered.

"Now, when anyone offers money for almost no work, I ask that question before anything else. And I never pay in order to earn."

qa.q: What did the stranger ask Avni to pay to activate the account?
qa.a: The stranger asked for a small deposit.

qa.q: Why did Avni put in more money after the first payout?
qa.a: The first payout made the offer feel real and touched Avni's hope, and greed followed when the stranger said bigger deposits paid more.

qa.q: What should Kashish check before replying to an offer like this?
qa.a: Ask why a stranger would give money away, check whether the company is registered, and never pay in order to earn.

qa.q: How might the stranger have seen the young Avni?
qa.a: As a hopeful person who could be drawn in with a small payout and then pushed to deposit more.

grounding: An easy remote-job offer works on Avni's hope and greed; Avni is left with the lesson to ask why a stranger would give money away and never pay to earn.

passage:
The waiting area of the bank branch smelled of floor cleaner. Naveen took a token and waited an hour before Suraj, the customer service executive, glanced up.

"Fraud? A ticket will be raised. Wait for the email," Suraj said, without looking at the papers Naveen had brought. Naveen felt hot with irritation and a helpless sinking.

"Could I have the ticket number in writing, please?"

A printed slip came out. A week later there was still no reply. Naveen sat down with a folder: the slip, screenshots, transaction details, the dates of every call. A formal complaint went out by email, with a stamped copy handed in at the branch. When the promised time passed, Naveen escalated to the bank's nodal officer and noted the ombudsman as the next step if it stalled.

Slowly the answers came. "Not warm," Naveen told a friend, "but paper works."

qa.q: What did Naveen ask Suraj to provide in writing?
qa.a: Naveen asked for the ticket number in writing.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the response at the counter?
qa.a: Naveen felt hot with irritation and a helpless sinking, as Suraj did not even look at the papers.

qa.q: What could Naveen do if the nodal officer's reply also stalls?
qa.a: Keep the folder organised, follow up in writing, and escalate to the ombudsman as already noted.

qa.q: What might it be like for Suraj at that counter?
qa.a: Suraj may be handling a long queue of routine tickets, which could explain the flat reply, though the passage does not say why Suraj was so brief.

grounding: After a fraud, the bank's support is slow and cold; Naveen stays organised with written complaints and escalation.

passage:
Irawati's phone buzzed for the fourth time before lunch: an unknown number, the loan app's recovery team. Her stomach tightened. "Pay today or we will message your contacts," said the latest voicemail.

In the office pantry she whispered to her colleague Asif, "I keep thinking of taking a loan from a different app to clear this one."

"Don't," Asif said. "That's how it stacks up." He suggested she save every call log and voicemail, note the times, and go to her bank about a repayment plan. "And threats like that are harassment, Irawati. It can be reported."

She opened a notes file and began listing the date, the number and what was said. Her hands slowed. She would ask the bank for an appointment first thing tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the latest voicemail threaten?
qa.a: It said that if she did not pay today they would message her contacts.

qa.q: What was Irawati tempted to do, and what does it show about her state?
qa.a: She was tempted to take a loan from a different app to clear this one, which shows how anxious and cornered she felt.

qa.q: What should Irawati do next?
qa.a: Save the call logs and voicemails, note dates and times, talk to the bank about a repayment plan, and report the harassment.

qa.q: How does Asif see the idea of a second loan?
qa.a: Asif sees it as a trap, since that is how debt stacks up.

grounding: Calls from a loan app's recovery team make Irawati anxious; a colleague steers her to keep records, talk to the bank and avoid a new loan.

passage:
Looking back, the numbers were never as frightening as the secret. For a year I paid my credit card minimum and two EMIs and told my family my salary was "tight but fine". At dinner I laughed in the right places and felt like a stranger.

One Sunday I finally wrote every due on paper: the card, the phone EMI, the two-wheeler EMI, with the interest beside each. The card's interest was the highest, so that became the first target.

Then I told my sister Ira. She was quiet for a second and said, "Show me the list." She didn't lecture. She sat with me while I called the card company.

The debt didn't vanish, but the loneliness did.

Aadhya

qa.q: What did Aadhya tell the family about the salary?
qa.a: Aadhya told them it was "tight but fine".

qa.q: Why did Aadhya feel like a stranger at dinner?
qa.a: Hiding the EMIs and card dues made Aadhya feel cut off, laughing in the right places while carrying a secret.

qa.q: Which steps made the debt more manageable for Aadhya?
qa.a: Writing every due on paper with its interest, going after the highest-interest card first, and telling one trusted person.

qa.q: What does Ira's reaction suggest about how Ira saw the news?
qa.a: Ira went quiet for a second, asked to see the list and did not lecture, which suggests Ira cared more about helping than blaming.

grounding: Aadhya hides EMIs and card dues from family, then faces the numbers on paper, prioritises the highest interest and tells a trusted person.

passage:
Monday. Madhuri's phone rang eleven times before noon. A rough voice from a recovery office said, "Pay tonight, or we will call everyone in your contact list and tell them you're a cheat." The room seemed to tilt, and Madhuri almost transferred the money right then.

Wednesday. A colleague showed Madhuri a message from an unknown number that mentioned a debt. Shaking, Madhuri called Gurpreet, who said, "This is harassment, and it is not your fault. Don't pay in panic. Save every call log." They screenshotted the logs together.

Saturday. With Gurpreet beside Madhuri, a complaint went to the bank, then to the ombudsman's portal, and a copy of the screenshots went to the police. The calls did not stop at once, but that night Madhuri slept without the phone on the pillow.

qa.q: How many times did the phone ring before noon on Monday?
qa.a: The phone rang eleven times before noon on Monday.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri almost transfer the money on Monday?
qa.a: The threat to call everyone in the contact list and call Madhuri a cheat caused panic.

qa.q: What steps did Madhuri take to answer the harassment?
qa.a: Saved call logs and screenshots, complained to the bank, filed on the ombudsman's portal, gave the police a copy, and did not pay in panic.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet's words change the way Madhuri saw the situation?
qa.a: Gurpreet named it harassment and said it was not Madhuri's fault, so panic gave way to a plan.

grounding: Recovery agents threaten to call Madhuri's contacts; over several days Madhuri keeps records, does not pay in panic and reports the harassment properly.

passage:
Zubin: Amma asked again about money for the cousin's wedding gift.
Ritu: I know. I'm still paying the loan I took for the house repairs.
Ritu: I keep saying yes because I can't say no to her face 😔
Zubin: You don't have to send what you don't have.
Ritu: They think my job pays double.
Zubin: Because they've never heard the real numbers.
Ritu: True. Papa keeps telling relatives I'm doing so well.
Zubin: Tell them your EMI and what's left after rent. I'll be there.
Ritu: Sunday lunch?
Zubin: Sunday lunch. Bring the numbers 🙂
Ritu: Okay. This much for the loan, this much for rent, this much I can give each month, and no more.
Zubin: That's a plan. Say it just like that.

qa.q: What does Ritu say the family thinks about her job?
qa.a: Ritu says they think her job pays double.

qa.q: Why does Ritu keep saying yes to Amma?
qa.a: Ritu cannot say no to Amma's face, so duty keeps winning even though the loan is a strain.

qa.q: What plan does Ritu make for Sunday lunch?
qa.a: Tell the family the real numbers: the loan, the rent and what can be given each month, and no more.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Ritu's situation?
qa.a: Zubin sees the family's belief as coming from never having heard the real numbers, and offers to be there when Ritu says them.

grounding: Ritu took a loan partly to meet family expectations and feels trapped; with Zubin's support Ritu plans to state limits and a repayment plan openly.

passage:
"You didn't answer my message," Raghav said, opening the door.

"I know. I'm sorry. I've been avoiding you and it's been eating me up," Vidya said. "I can't pay the full amount this month. The landlord raised the rent."

"Okay. Thank you for telling me straight."

"I can give you this much now." Vidya held out an envelope. "The rest on the first of the next two months. I'll message you the day before each time."

Raghav took it. "I'd rather hear about a delay than get silence."

"You were there when I needed it, and I don't want money to make you feel used."

"It won't. Now come in, the tea's getting cold."

qa.q: Why can't Vidya pay the full amount this month?
qa.a: The landlord raised the rent.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel while avoiding Raghav?
qa.a: Vidya felt guilty and worn down, saying it had been eating Vidya up.

qa.q: What could Vidya keep doing to protect the friendship while repaying?
qa.a: Message Raghav the day before each instalment and tell the truth early about any delay.

qa.q: How does Raghav see the missed reply?
qa.a: Raghav would rather hear about a delay than get silence, and is glad Vidya told the matter straight.

grounding: Vidya repays a friend's crisis loan honestly: says openly that the full sum is late, offers a plan and does not avoid the friend.

passage:
Tuesday. Hafsa scrolled past Noor's photos from a weekend trip. Noor still owed the money Hafsa had lent in March for exam fees, and every text about it got a "will do soon!" Hafsa felt used, and a bit petty for counting.

Thursday. Hafsa wrote one clear message: "I need the money back. Could you pay half by the end of the month and half a month after? Tell me if that doesn't work." The reply came two hours later: "Sorry, I've been dodging you. Yes."

The following Sunday. Half arrived. Over tea Hafsa said, "I still like you a lot, but from now on I'll only lend what I can afford to lose." Noor nodded, embarrassed. The friendship felt smaller than before, but more honest.

qa.q: What did Hafsa propose in the message?
qa.a: Hafsa proposed that Noor pay half by the end of the month and half a month after.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel on Tuesday, and why?
qa.a: Hafsa felt used and a bit petty for counting, because Noor was on a trip while still owing the money.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do to lend more safely in future?
qa.a: Lend only what can be lost without harm, as Hafsa said over tea.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt writing "I've been dodging you"?
qa.a: Noor was probably embarrassed and a little guilty, which matches the embarrassed nod later over tea.

grounding: Hafsa lent money and Noor keeps dodging; Hafsa feels used, asks once clearly with a plan and decides what to lend in future.

passage:
Dear Karthik,

Remember the phone I said I "had to" upgrade? I did it: nothing down, twelve small EMIs, "only a few hundred a month". Then the headphones, then the jacket, each on its own tiny EMI. Last night I finally added them all in a note and the total surprised me. Small EMIs stack up quietly 😅

I asked myself the question you would ask: do I need it? Honestly, none of those was a need. They were a mood, and my friends' new things. So I've made a rule: any purchase waits a week. If I still want it after that, I look at the total cost, not the monthly figure. And no new EMI until two of these are cleared.

Thanks for not laughing when I told you.

Asif

qa.q: How many small EMIs did the phone purchase involve?
qa.a: The phone came with twelve small EMIs.

qa.q: What did Asif realise on adding up the EMIs?
qa.a: Asif was surprised at the total and saw that none of the purchases was a need; they came from a mood and from friends' new things.

qa.q: What rule did Asif set to avoid more debt for lifestyle spending?
qa.a: Any purchase waits a week, then the total cost is checked, and no new EMI is taken until two of the existing ones are cleared.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Karthik may feel trusted for being told honestly, since Asif thanks Karthik for not laughing.

grounding: Easy credit and buy-now-pay-later feel harmless to Asif until small EMIs are tallied; Asif asks about need and delays purchases.

passage:
Deepak had just put the plates on the table when Mahima said, "I need to tell you something, and I need you to let me finish." A personal loan, taken a year ago, was still owed. Mahima had been paying it quietly out of savings.

"Why didn't you tell me?" The words came out sharper than he meant. It was not the amount that stung. It was that he had been the last to know, and the past year replayed in his head, every time he had asked whether things were fine.

He breathed in and pushed his plate aside. "Okay. Show me everything: the lender, the interest, what's left."

Mahima brought the papers. By eleven they had a repayment plan on the fridge and a new rule: any debt, of any size, gets said out loud within a week.

qa.q: How long ago was the personal loan taken?
qa.a: The loan was taken a year ago.

qa.q: What is Deepak feeling as the past year replays in his head, and why?
qa.a: Hurt, mostly by the secrecy: Deepak was the last to know, and the amount was not what stung.

qa.q: What steps helped them handle the news?
qa.a: Deepak listened, asked for the full picture, and they made a repayment plan and agreed a rule to speak up about any debt within a week.

qa.q: What might it be like for Mahima to hand over the papers?
qa.a: Probably a mix of relief and nervousness, since Mahima asked to be allowed to finish speaking and then brought the papers when asked.

grounding: Mahima reveals a hidden debt; Deepak is hurt mainly by the secrecy, then listens, asks for the full picture and makes a shared plan.
